title: When Power Takes the Church: What History Keeps Showing Us
subtitle: From Constantine to apartheid, the recurring bargain in which the church trades its independent voice for a place beside power, and the few who refused to make it.

sections.title: The Bargain the Church Keeps Making
sections.body:
There is a story the church loves to tell about itself, in which the world is the threat and the faith is the victim, forever besieged from outside. The record tells a different story. The gravest wounds to the church's witness have rarely come from persecution. They have come from success, from the moment a ruler stopped killing Christians and started courting them, and the church discovered how good it felt to be wanted by power. That is the pattern this piece walks. Not one scandal but a recurring bargain, struck in different centuries and different tongues, always with the same terms and the same cost.

The terms are simple. Power offers the church legitimacy, protection, a seat at the table, the feeling that history is finally moving its way. In return the church lends power the one thing power cannot buy, a blessing, the language of God laid over a human agenda, the assurance that this cause is holy. The trade looks like a gain every single time it is made. It is a gain, for a while. What quietly gets spent is the only thing the church exists to keep, the freedom to speak a word its patrons did not write.

I am not describing someone else's sin. I am describing a temptation with no party and no century, one that finds the conservative and the progressive by different doors and leaves both holding the same empty hands. So before we walk the cases, name the thing we are watching for. Not the church attacked. The church flattered. It is the second that has done the deeper damage, because the second lets us keep everything except the reason we were sent.

sections.title: When the Emperor Became a Friend
sections.body:
For nearly three centuries the church was an illegal thing, its members liable to confiscation, exile, and death. Then in 313 the emperor Constantine and his co-ruler Licinius agreed at Milan to let Christians worship without penalty, and within a single lifetime the faith of the catacombs had become the faith of the court. Bishops who had expected prison received tax exemptions and basilicas. By 380, under Theodosius, Christianity was not merely legal but the official religion of the empire, and the hunted outsider had become the establishment.

Something real was gained. The persecuted found peace. The poor were fed by a church now rich enough to feed them, and the moral vocabulary of the gospel began to work its way into Roman law. But something was traded, and the trade is the whole point. A church that had once spoken to power from outside now spoke from inside it, its bishops dependent on imperial favor, its councils convened and sometimes bullied by emperors with opinions about God. The voice that had said no to Caesar learned to say the prayers at his coronation.

The historian Peter Brown has spent a career complicating the tidy version of this story, showing that the change was slower, messier, and less total than the phrase a Constantinian fall suggests, that old loyalties lingered and the new order stayed contested for generations. He is right to distrust the melodrama. The church was not corrupted in an afternoon. But the shape was set at Milan, the altar placed beside the throne, and every later bargain in this piece is a variation on the one first struck there.

sections.title: The Cross Fitted to the Swastika
sections.body:
The most naked modern version came in Germany. As Hitler rose, a movement called the German Christians, the Deutsche Christen, set out to weld the Protestant faith to National Socialism, to recast Jesus as an Aryan hero and the church as an organ of the Reich. They pressed to apply the Aryan paragraph inside the church itself, purging pastors of Jewish descent from their pulpits, and they cheered as a Reich bishop was installed to bring the German soul under one flag and one Lord who grew harder each year to tell apart from the Fuhrer.

They were not a fringe. They won church elections and wielded real power, and the sober fact the record presses on us is that most German Protestants went along, by conviction or by silence. The resisters were the minority. But there was a minority. In 1934 a body of pastors met at Barmen and issued a declaration, drafted principally by Karl Barth, confessing that Jesus Christ is the one Word of God the church must hear and obey in life and in death, and rejecting the claim that any other power or event could stand beside him as a second revelation. It was a flat theological no to the state's total demand.

Out of that refusal grew the Confessing Church, and names that cost their bearers everything, Bonhoeffer hanged, Niemoller imprisoned for years. Read Eberhard Bethge on Bonhoeffer and Robert Ericksen on the theologians who went the other way, and the lesson is not that Christians resisted. It is that so few did, and that the machinery of a captured church was built and run by the baptized.

sections.title: A Bible Enlisted for the Auction Block
sections.body:
Cross the ocean and step back a century, and the same bargain spoke with an American accent. Here the church did not serve a dictator. It served an economy, and it read its Bible to defend that economy at the root. Learned ministers stood in respectable pulpits and argued that Scripture plainly sanctioned the holding of human beings as property, that the patriarchs owned slaves and the apostle Paul returned a runaway to his master, that the peculiar institution was ordained and the abolitionist was the true infidel wresting the text.

The historian Mark Noll has named what came of this a theological crisis. On a flat, proof-texting reading of the Bible, the defenders of slavery held the easier ground, verse for verse, and the churches could not settle by argument what the nation finally settled by war. A faith that had made itself chaplain to a slave society could no longer summon the authority to condemn it, because it had already sold that authority for its place in Southern respectability.

The counter-voice did not rise mainly from the comfortable. It rose from Frederick Douglass, who had felt the lash under masters who prayed, and who drew a line that still cuts. He set the Christianity of Christ against what he called the Christianity of this land, refusing to let the religion of the slaveholder keep the name of the crucified. He did not abandon the faith. He indicted the counterfeit in the name of the real, and that distinction is the argument of this whole piece, spoken by a man the church of his day would not free.

sections.title: A Theology Built to Keep Men Apart
sections.body:
In the twentieth century the pattern found Afrikaner South Africa. After the National Party took power in 1948 it built apartheid, a whole legal order of racial separation, and it did not build the thing alone. The white Dutch Reformed Church supplied the theology, teaching that God himself had divided the nations at Babel and willed the races to develop apart, that separation was not sin but the created order obeyed. The gospel of one new humanity in Christ was pressed into the service of a state built on keeping that humanity sorted by skin.

Again the counter-witness came from the inside. Beyers Naude was an Afrikaner minister and a member of the secret Broederbond, a son of the establishment who read the same Bible and could no longer make it say what his church needed said. He broke with apartheid theology, was stripped of his standing and silenced under banning orders, and paid with his place among his own people. Alongside him Desmond Tutu, from the Anglican side, kept naming the arrangement as sin while naming it was still dangerous.

The wider Reformed communion at last declared the theological defense of apartheid a heresy, and in 1986 the daughter church confessed against it in the Belhar Confession, binding unity and reconciliation and justice into the creed itself. John de Gruchy has told this church struggle with the honesty it deserves, including the long years the churches were complicit before a few grew brave. The heresy was no foreign import. It was preached in the mother tongue, by men who loved their people and mistook that love for the will of God.

sections.title: The Same Bargain, Wearing Our Colors
sections.body:
Set the four cases side by side and the shape is unmistakable. Milan, Berlin, the Southern pulpit, the Afrikaner synod. Different centuries, different politics, one bargain. The church is offered power on the condition that it bless what power already means to do, and each time enough of the church says yes to make refusal a minority act. The tragedy is never that the world was too strong. It is that the blessing was too sweet, and the God invoked too useful to question.

Now the hard turn, because it would be a lie to file all this under other people's history. This temptation keeps no party. The right conscripts the cross for the nation and calls the flag holy, and that is idolatry, and I have watched my own tribe do it and stay quiet far too long. The left can perform the identical move from the other direction, dissolving the gospel into whatever the moment's politics already wanted until the church is a chaplaincy to a cause, with no word the cause has not already approved. Both trades feel like relevance. Both spend the same coin. A church that can only ever bless one side has already told you which lord it truly fears.

The witnesses in every case were few, and they were rarely heroic by temperament. They were people who kept one thing back from the bargain, the freedom to say that Christ is Lord and Caesar is not, whatever Caesar happens to be calling himself this year. That freedom is the entire inheritance. And we keep trading it for a seat at a table that was never ours. The record does not leave us asking whether they failed. It leaves us asking whether we can hear what their refusal cost them, and go make the same trade this afternoon.
